source: Gibson and Birkinshaw (2004) working paper version, Contextual determinants of organisational ambidexterity (AMJ 47:209)
finding: Business units high in both alignment and adaptability performed best. Contextual ambidexterity, not unit separation, was the mechanism studied.
numbers: 41 business units, 10 multinationals, 4234 survey respondents (published paper says 4195). Four groups, mean performance on 7-point scale: aligned 3.21, adaptive 3.74, moderately ambidextrous 4.10, highly ambidextrous 4.60. ANOVA F=18.11, p<.001; all pairwise differences significant (SNK).
limits: Cross-sectional survey, unit-level n=41, perceptual performance, groups made by splits not a continuous model.
agent_relevance: Doing both in one unit beat specialising in one. Weak evidence base for any design rule.

source: Gibson and Birkinshaw (2004) working paper version, Contextual determinants of organisational ambidexterity (AMJ 47:209)
finding: Robustness check with different respondents rating each construct kept the ranking but weakened the top contrast.
numbers: Senior raters for performance, junior raters for alignment and adaptability: means 3.41, 3.88, 4.11, 4.13; F=5.57, p<.01; top two groups no longer significantly different. Regrouping to fix single-company group 1: 3.42, 3.80, 4.14, 4.60; F=13.59, p<.001.
limits: Authors own check, not independent. Same-source bias was a stated worry.
agent_relevance: Gain from the highest ambidexterity level over the moderate level is fragile; most of the benefit is from not being one-sided.

source: Gibson and Birkinshaw (2004) working paper version, Contextual determinants of organisational ambidexterity (AMJ 47:209)
finding: Unit-level correlations link management-rated adaptability and alignment to performance. Alignment and adaptability are themselves positively correlated, so not strict trade-offs.
numbers: n=41 units. Performance with adaptability r=.78 (p<.01), with alignment r=.54 (p<.05); alignment with adaptability r=.54. Line-rated organisation context with performance r=.37; social context r=.45; performance-management context r=.27. Subjective vs peer-group financial performance r=.75 (p<.05).
limits: Same-source management ratings for the key variables inflate r. Context was line-rated, less inflated.
agent_relevance: The two demands can be positively related when context is supportive. Little causal weight.

source: Junni, Sarala, Taras and Tarba (2013) Organizational ambidexterity and performance: a meta-analysis
finding: Pooled ambidexterity-performance link is positive and significant but depends on context and method. Stronger in non-manufacturing, at higher levels of analysis, with combined (not balance) measures, perceptual performance and cross-sectional or multimethod designs.
numbers: AMP 27(4):299-312. Page gives no k, N or r. About 770 to 812 citations.
limits: Only the abstract page was read; effect sizes not seen. Method moderators suggest part of the effect is measurement artefact.
agent_relevance: The benefit is conditional. Treat any balance rule as per-environment, like the per-class settings in S0.

source: Mathias (2014) Exploration, exploitation, ambidexterity and firm performance: a meta-analysis (Emerald, vol 14, ch 12)
finding: Exploration and exploitation each have strong performance effects. Ambidexterity has a weaker effect than focusing on either alone, contrary to the received view.
numbers: 117 studies, more than 21,000 firms. No effect sizes on the page.
limits: Abstract page only. Different coding from Junni 2013. Author name comes from search results, not the page.
agent_relevance: Counter-evidence: a focused mode may beat a split one. Argues against a mandatory explore stage.

source: Mathias, McKenny and Crook (2018) Managing the tensions between exploration and exploitation: the role of time (SEJ 12:316)
finding: Ambidexterity helps more in older firms and when balance runs across the whole organisation. Weaker when ambidexterity is measured dynamically and when performance is long-term.
numbers: 52 studies, more than 13,000 organisational observations.
limits: Abstract page only. No effect sizes seen.
agent_relevance: Gains show in short-run measures and shrink over long horizons. Relevant to judging a scheme on one run.

source: Meta-analysis, Too small to do it all? Exploration, exploitation and ambidexterity with SME performance (J Business Research 132:653, 2021)
finding: In small firms ambidexterity relates less strongly to performance than either exploration or exploitation alone. Property-rights protection weakens both single-orientation links.
numbers: 5,488 SMEs, 34 studies. No effect sizes on the page.
limits: Abstract page only. SME sample. Author names not shown on the page.
agent_relevance: Resource-limited systems may do better focused. Fits a small-budget agent.

source: Kula (2023) Identifying the innovative tension: a meta-analysis on innovative firm behavior, ambidexterity and innovative performance (Isletme Arastirmalari Dergisi 15:593)
finding: Ambidexterity has a large pooled link to innovative performance by the author labels.
numbers: Dataset 2: 22 studies, 49 effects, N=98,630; Hedges g=0.771, 95% CI 0.639 to 0.903, Z=11.47. Dataset 1 (innovative behaviour to ambidexterity): 19 studies, 30 effects, N=11,246; g=0.783, CI 0.622 to 0.943. Egger test: no publication bias.
limits: g near 0.77 is very large for survey data and sits oddly beside Mathias 2014; likely inflated by common-source perceptual measures. Outcome is innovative performance, not financial.
agent_relevance: The literature depends on the outcome measure. Do not trust one pooled effect.

source: Wikipedia, Organizational ambidexterity (overview)
finding: Field summary: structural, contextual and sequential forms; structural-vs-contextual question unresolved.
numbers: Cites Gibson and Birkinshaw 2004 (41 units), Chandrasekaran 2012 (34 high-tech firms), He and Wong 2004 (interaction positive for sales growth, imbalance negative), British Airways 1981 to 1986 case.
limits: Encyclopedia. Some claims tagged citation needed.
agent_relevance: Orientation only. Verify against primary sources.

source: Wikipedia, Organizational ambidexterity (boundary conditions)
finding: A balanced orientation did not significantly help when environmental munificence was low. Market orientation raised the benefit; without it ambidextrous firms had lower financial performance. Small firms without slack may do better one-sided.
numbers: No numbers on the page.
limits: Second-hand summary.
agent_relevance: Match balance to environment and resources, the per-class idea.

source: Wikipedia, Organizational ambidexterity (structural vs contextual)
finding: No head-to-head test settles structural versus contextual. Structural suits long stable periods broken by rare discontinuities. Firms in dynamic and competitive settings lean contextual.
numbers: No numbers. Some researchers say inconsistent structures lower performance.
limits: Encyclopedia summary.
agent_relevance: Separate sub-agents versus one agent with both modes is open even in the source field.

source: Jansen, Van den Bosch and Volberda (2006) Exploratory innovation, exploitative innovation, and performance (Management Science 52:1661)
finding: Centralisation hurts exploratory innovation. Formalisation helps exploitative innovation. Connectedness helps both. Exploration pays more in dynamic environments; exploitation pays more in competitive ones.
numbers: About 2,968 citations (Crossref). Sample sizes not read.
limits: Abstract only, from Crossref. Full text blocked (403).
agent_relevance: Environment decides which mode pays. Supports conditional switching.

source: Cao, Gedajlovic and Zhang (2009) Unpacking organizational ambidexterity (Organization Science 20:781)
finding: Balance and combined magnitude are separate dimensions with different mechanisms. Both high together gives extra benefit. Balance helps resource-poor firms; combined magnitude helps resource-rich firms.
numbers: About 1,246 citations. Effect sizes not read.
limits: Abstract only, from Crossref.
agent_relevance: Explains mixed results: findings flip with the measure and the resource level.

source: Raisch and Birkinshaw (2008) Organizational ambidexterity: antecedents, outcomes, and moderators (J Management 34:375)
finding: Review model of antecedents, moderators and outcomes, with gaps noted across research domains.
numbers: About 1,895 citations.
limits: Abstract only, from Crossref.
agent_relevance: Background map. No agent-specific result.

source: Chandrasekaran et al. (2012), cited in Wikipedia
finding: Simultaneous exploration and exploitation associated with higher performance in high-tech organisations.
numbers: 34 high-tech organisations, per Wikipedia (tagged citation needed).
limits: Not opened; second-hand.
agent_relevance: Small sample.

source: He and Wong (2004), cited in Wikipedia
finding: Interaction of exploration and exploitation related positively to sales growth; imbalance related negatively.
numbers: No numbers seen. The JSTOR page failed to load.
limits: Not opened; second-hand.
agent_relevance: Supports a balance-needed reading, but a firm survey.

source: Krishnamurthy, Harris, Foster, Zhang and Slivkins (2024) Can large language models explore in-context?
finding: Out of the box, LLMs fail to explore in a multi-armed bandit. Only GPT-4 with chain of thought and an externally summarised history explored well.
numbers: Hard instance K=5 arms, gap 0.2. GPT-4 basic prompt, T=500, N=20: more than 60% of runs never picked the best arm after early rounds (suffix failure), like Greedy. Good configuration: T=200, N=40, very few suffix failures. Main sweep T=100; GPT-3.5 N=20 over 48 prompts.
limits: Simple bandit, not an organisation. Success needed external summarisation.
agent_relevance: LLMs default to exploitation; a scaffold must supply exploration explicitly.

source: Krishnamurthy, Harris, Foster, Zhang and Slivkins (2024) Can large language models explore in-context?
finding: Second failure mode: uniform-like behaviour, spreading choices over all arms without dropping bad ones.
numbers: Only three GPT-4 configurations avoided suffix failures at T=100; two of them failed in uniform-like ways; one succeeded. Suffix failures measurable with T=100 and 10 to 20 replicates.
limits: Same study. Failures are prompt-dependent.
agent_relevance: Both too little and too much exploration occur; test per class.

source: Nie et al. (2024) EVOLvE: evaluating and optimizing LLMs for exploration (ICML 2025)
finding: Algorithm-guided support and algorithm distillation let smaller models explore better than larger ones on several bandit tasks.
numbers: Regret analysis links exploration ability to model size and the algorithm. No numbers on the abstract page.
limits: Abstract only. Fine-tuning route, not scaffold-only.
agent_relevance: An external classical explorer beats asking the model to explore; matches structural separation.

source: Schmied et al. (2025) LLMs are greedy agents: effects of RL fine-tuning on decision-making abilities
finding: LLM agents show greediness, frequency bias and a knowing-doing gap. RL fine-tuning on self-generated reasoning increases exploration and narrows the gap.
numbers: Tasks: multi-armed bandits, contextual bandits, tic-tac-toe. No numbers on the abstract page.
limits: Abstract only.
agent_relevance: Greediness is a default; an explicit explore operator counters it, but fine-tuning is the tested fix.

source: Multi-Agent LLMs Fail to Explore Each Other (arXiv 2607.11250, 2026)
finding: LLM agents choosing peers commit early to one peer, sometimes the worse one. A LinUCB-style peer selector (MACE) reduces regret.
numbers: Two-armed delegation: pA=0.6, pB=0.5, T=50, 30 runs; Qwen2.5-7B, GPT-4, GPT-5 bimodal; UCB concentrates on the better peer. GPT-5 picks Qwen-7B 294 of 297 times under in-context exploration. Regret O(sqrt(T log T)) for MACE, Omega(T) for greedy.
limits: Peer-selection task, not a structural-vs-contextual test. Single paper, no replication.
agent_relevance: The in-context (contextual) route to balance failed; an external bandit controller worked.

source: Multi-Agent LLMs Fail to Explore Each Other (arXiv 2607.11250, 2026)
finding: On HotpotQA with 10 agents holding partial context, MACE beats in-context exploration, random and fixed neighbours.
numbers: Final round, exploration phase, EM/F1: MACE 0.3133/0.3941; in-context 0.2257/0.2810; pre-defined 0.2700/0.3370; random 0.2733/0.3338. Exploitation phase: MACE 0.2687/0.3415; in-context 0.2433/0.3001; random 0.2383/0.3053. 600 hard samples, R=5.
limits: In-context exploration was worse than random.
agent_relevance: Asking the model to self-balance did worse than chance; explicit structure won.

source: Multi-Agent LLMs Fail to Explore Each Other (arXiv 2607.11250, 2026)
finding: Benefit carries to math and science QA and transfers to another dataset with frozen parameters.
numbers: Math500 L4-5 accuracy, explore/exploit phase: MACE 0.6450/0.6832; in-context 0.6183/0.6031; random 0.5611/0.5763. GPQA Diamond: MACE 0.5404/0.5758; in-context 0.4343/0.4596; random 0.4747/0.4394. 2WikiMultihopQA transfer EM/F1: MACE 0.1820/0.1987; in-context 0.1227/0.1375; random 0.1623/0.1784.
limits: Pooled mixed models (GPT-5, Qwen, Llama, Mistral). Per-round tables only partly read.
agent_relevance: Learned exploration pays most in the later exploitation phase; cost shows up first.

source: Kula (2023) meta-analysis, heterogeneity and bias tests
finding: The author used a random-effects model because of heterogeneity and found no publication bias on the Egger test, yet the pooled effect is much larger than other meta-analyses report.
numbers: Dataset 1 Egger intercept 2.422; dataset 2 total 49 effects from 22 studies, N=98,630. Studies published since 2000 only.
limits: Only English and Turkish-accessible databases used by one author; no moderator analysis of structure type. Contrast with Mathias 2014 (ambidexterity weaker than focus) is unresolved.
agent_relevance: Different coders reach opposite conclusions on the same literature, so no single pooled number should set an agent parameter.

source: Gibson and Birkinshaw (2004) working paper version, what produces ambidexterity
finding: Ambidexterity was tied to a context mixing performance management (stretch and discipline) with social context (support and trust). Aligned-only units were especially low on performance management context.
numbers: Context groups differed by ANOVA: performance management context F=4.16 (p=.004), social context F=4.14 (p=.01), combined organisation context F=5.41 (p=.003). Line-rated social context correlates r=.68 with performance management context.
limits: n=41 units; context measured by line staff but the mechanism is inferred from cross-sectional data.
agent_relevance: Suggests balance comes from the surrounding rules and trust, not from a separate unit. For an agent, the prompt context that sets both discipline and freedom may matter more than splitting roles.
